summary.statement: US website accessibility lawsuits are frequent and rising: 3,117 federal filings in 2025 (+27%) and 5,000+ across federal and state courts, about 70% against e-commerce.
Repeat suits are common: 1,427 2025 suits hit previously sued companies, and a Shopify merchant reports three suits in four years.
Costs are material for small stores: settlements typically $15k-$75k, and a three-employee brand faced a $30k demand.
Exposure is uneven: larger companies are a growing share of defendants, some states add small-business safe harbors, and California courts largely exclude online-only businesses.
Many target-profile beauty and apparel stores rely on overlay widgets (UserWay, accessiBe, Accessibly) as their accessibility solution.
Overlays do not stop lawsuits: about 38% of 2025 defendants already had a tool installed, and widget users were sued every month.
Merchants report being sued while running overlays and then turning to code fixes by freelancers.
Regulators and the disability community reject overlays as compliance (FTC order on accessiBe; EDF/IAAP statement; practitioner letter).
In small stores the owner handles accessibility personally and often does not know whom to hire.
Many organisations keep accessibility in-house but lack the expertise to sustain it.
No public evidence found on how stores in the $500k-$50M band budget for accessibility or which role signs off.
Demand letters and lawsuits are the main trigger; vendors build products for the moment a letter arrives, and merchants install tools right after being sued.
The EAA brings e-commerce into scope and the Dutch regulator has sent letters to e-commerce firms worldwide.
Urgency is dampened by weak early EAA enforcement, a microenterprise exemption, and notice-and-cure reforms that give time to fix after notice.
Remediation is quoted at about $4k-$25k, and an agency estimates $3k-$10k for an audit plus $5k-$25k for fixes.
Small stores lack developer capacity; one merchant is hiring a freelance coder after three lawsuits.
One agency says compliance is not a major undertaking for a mid-market brand.
No evidence found on actual internal developer hours spent on accessibility.
Source-code remediation for Shopify is already crowded: TestParty, Curbcut, AccessComply, Remedy, AccessFix, Patrol and AI operators like Fudge, at $49-$599/month.
Some overlay buyers are satisfied with price and ease, and some merchants see the overlay debate as 50/50, weakening the switching trigger.
Merchants distrust monthly-fee compliance vendors after lawsuits, a barrier for a subscription offer.
Removing an overlay is easy, but merchants who drop one still have to do the code work.
E-commerce is the most-sued sector, and an apparel retailer's complaint grew into a $5.15M class settlement.
Image-heavy catalogs fail on product alt text, the top finding in small WooCommerce store audits including clothing brands.
Shopify's standard checkout is platform-controlled and tested against WCAG, so checkout fixes are less of a merchant-side opportunity on Shopify.

hypothesis_update.problem: US and EU e-commerce stores (especially apparel and beauty on Shopify/WooCommerce) face frequent, repeat accessibility lawsuits and new EAA obligations; the overlay widgets many of them pay for do not prevent suits, and they lack in-house developer capacity to fix theme code.
hypothesis_update.users: Owners and e-commerce managers of small and mid-size Shopify and WooCommerce stores, and the agencies that build and maintain them.
hypothesis_update.buyer: Store owner or head of e-commerce; for agencies, the agency owner.
hypothesis_update.decision_maker: In small stores the owner decides, usually after a demand letter or lawsuit; no public evidence yet on budget ownership in mid-size stores.
hypothesis_update.economic_value: Avoid settlements (typically $15k-$75k, repeat suits common), EAA exposure, and $5k-$25k one-off agency remediation; replace overlay subscriptions that do not prevent suits.
hypothesis_update.industry: E-commerce, with apparel, beauty and consumer goods as early focus

rationale.statement: Lawsuits are frequent, rising and concentrated on e-commerce, with many repeat defendants.
About 38% of 2025 defendants already had an accessibility tool, and widget users were sued every month.
Small stores lack money and expertise to hire developers for remediation.
The source-code remediation niche is already crowded, so the problem is real but differentiation is the open question.

new_unknowns.question: What would make a merchant choose this product over existing Shopify source-remediation apps (TestParty, Curbcut, AccessComply, Patrol) at similar prices?
Will notice-and-cure laws (e.g., Missouri 2026) and weak early EAA enforcement reduce merchants' willingness to pay before receiving a demand letter?

current_solutions.statement: Many small and mid-size stores install overlay widgets (UserWay, accessiBe, Accessibly) and publish accessibility statements.
After lawsuits, merchants hire freelancers or agencies to fix theme code, at quoted costs of about $4k-$25k.
A growing set of Shopify apps already fix accessibility in theme source code (TestParty, Curbcut, AccessComply, Remedy, Patrol).
Shopify covers part of the problem natively with accessible themes, alt-text generation and a WCAG-tested checkout.
